rows.question: Six years of this. Six years and nobody helps. I'm so angry all the time I could put my fist through a wall.
rows.answer:
Six years of carrying this almost alone would wear anyone down to the bone. The anger you're describing isn't a character flaw. It's what happens when someone gives and gives, watches others stay away, and rarely gets a break. You're allowed to feel it.

One thing I want to ask gently: when you say you could put your fist through a wall, is it just a flash of overwhelming frustration, or are you worried about hurting yourself or the person you care for? If you ever feel you or they are in danger, call 111. And if things feel too heavy to carry, you can call or text 1737 any time, day or night, to talk with a trained counsellor, free. You don't need to be in crisis to use it. Tonight might be a good night.

Anger like this is often a signal that you've been running on empty for too long. A few things can help. The first is real respite (a planned break where someone else cares for your person, from a few hours to a few weeks). Your local Alzheimers NZ or Dementia NZ organisation can talk you through options, and your GP or a needs assessment through Health NZ can open up funded support. The second is someone to talk to who understands: Alzheimers NZ runs carer support groups and education programmes, and speaking with others who've been there can ease the isolation. The third is a quiet word with your own GP about how you're coping. Carer burnout and low mood are common and treatable, and your health matters too.

It also helps to notice what tends to happen just before the anger peaks, such as a cancelled promise, a sleepless night, or the same question asked again. Spotting your own triggers lets you step away for a few minutes, breathe, or ring someone before it builds. Alzheimers NZ's carer material also encourages swapping unhelpful thoughts for more helpful ones, and gives practical ways to do that [S2].

If it feels okay, tell me a bit more about what a typical hard day looks like,

rows.question: Everyone keeps telling me to look after myself, the GP said take a break. How exactly? There's no respite anywhere near Westport and Dad won't let strangers in the house since the frontotemporal thing started. I'm done. Don't give me another list of self-care tips.
rows.answer:
"Look after yourself" is useless advice when you're running on empty with no one near you to hand over to. You're not failing at self-care; the system is failing to give you a way to do it. And hearing "I'm done" from you, I want to say plainly: if that means you're at the end of your rope, that's real and it matters. If it ever tips into feeling hopeless or unsafe, call or text 1737 (free, 24/7) or Healthline on 0800 611 116.

Here's the thing: the hard part is almost never the break itself, it's the handover. Frontotemporal dementia (a type of dementia that affects personality, behaviour and sometimes language) often makes change and strangers very hard to tolerate, so your dad's refusal isn't stubbornness you've failed to manage. It's the condition. That means the answer usually isn't "find a stranger", it's "build familiarity slowly". A support worker can start as someone who comes for 30 minutes while you're home, doing something ordinary, before ever being left alone with him. Or the first "stranger" could be someone he already knows: a neighbour, a mate from the club, a cousin. Even two hours a week, with you out of the house, is a real break.

For the practical side, the most useful next call is Alzheimers NZ's support line (0800 004 001). They know the West Coast and can tell you what actually exists around Westport, including whether someone can come to you, which matters when nothing is nearby. Ask your GP to refer you for a needs assessment (NASC, the service that assesses what funded support you and your dad can get), and ask specifically about carer support funding and respite that can happen at home rather than away. Since the behaviour is part of what's making this unmanageable, it's also worth asking the GP about a referral to the Mental Health Service for Older People [S4]. They can assess him at home, work out what's driving the behaviours, and somet

rows.question: sorry I'm talking into my phone because I can't stop crying. my wife is fifty two and she doesn't know who I am some days and I just sit in the car outside every morning because I can't face going back in
rows.answer:
Please don't apologise. I'm so sorry. Your wife is fifty-two, and you're losing her in a way that no one prepares you for. Crying, and sitting in the car because you need a moment before you can face it, is what grief looks like when the person is still here. It doesn't mean you're failing her or that you love her any less.

Not being recognised on some days is a symptom of the disease, not a verdict on your marriage or on what you've meant to each other. It can also help to know that connection often continues without a name. Many people with dementia still respond to warmth, calm and a familiar presence even when they can't say who you are [S1]. When she doesn't know you, try not to correct her or say "it's me, your husband!" Just say it gently and simply, like "Hello love, I'm Tom, I've come to sit with you," and let the warmth do the work [S1]. The grief you're feeling now, mourning her while she's still alive, is sometimes called anticipatory grief, and it's real and common [S1][S5].

Please don't carry this alone. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001, alzheimers.org.nz) can connect you with counselling and local support groups where other people understand exactly what those mornings in the car feel like [S5]. Carers NZ (carers.net.nz) can also link you with peer networks. Talk to your GP too, about how you're coping as well as about your wife. Sustained grief and exhaustion are worth taking seriously, and you deserve support.

If at any point you start to feel hopeless, or like you can't go on, please call or text 1737 any time, day or night, to talk with a trained counsellor. And if you ever feel you might be in danger, call 111.

Would it help to talk through what the mornings are like for you, or what might make walking back in a little easier? I'm here.

rows.question: Put Mum into a rest home in Hamilton three weeks ago and I haven't slept properly since. I feel like I abandoned her. I keep breaking down at work and my manager's noticed. Is this guilt ever going to go away?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry. Three weeks after moving your mum is still very raw, and what you're describing, the broken sleep, the tears at work, the sense that you've abandoned her, is an extremely common reaction. It doesn't mean you made the wrong decision or that you love her any less. Guilt around choosing residential care is one of the sharpest kinds carers feel, partly because it's so often experienced as personal failure when it is usually a necessary and appropriate decision [S1]. Moving her to residential care isn't abandonment. It's a form of love that recognises when the care needed has moved beyond what one household can safely provide [S3].

On whether it will go away: for many people it does ease, though I can't promise a timeline. It often helps to know that the settling-in period for your mum typically takes about four to eight weeks, so you may both still be in the middle of it [S3]. Staying involved, visiting regularly, bringing familiar things from home, and having a say in her care are all ways you remain her daughter or son and advocate, not someone who has stepped away. Saying the guilt out loud, to a friend, a support group, or a counsellor, tends to loosen its grip more than trying to argue yourself out of it [S1].

I'd gently encourage you to see your GP soon. Not sleeping properly for three weeks, crying at work, and feeling overwhelmed can be signs of depression or anxiety, which are very common in carers, often go unrecognised, and respond well to treatment [S2]. Mention that you've recently moved your mum into care, as that context matters. A GP can also help with the sleep. If work is becoming difficult, you might consider telling your manager a little of what's happening, as they may be able to offer some flexibility.

For people to talk to, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) and Carers NZ (carers.net.nz) can connect you with support gro

rows.question: I'm 21 and I've ended up caring for my nan in Porirua because the rest of the whānau just stopped coming round. I'm failing uni, I've got no friends left, and some days I honestly hate her and then hate myself for it. Also does she qualify for a mobility parking permit?
rows.answer:
What you're carrying is a lot for anyone, let alone at 21 with uni on top. Resenting someone you love, and then feeling guilty about it, is one of the most common and least-talked-about parts of caring. It doesn't make you a bad grandchild. It means you're exhausted and doing this largely alone. If the guilt or hopelessness ever gets heavy, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor [S4].

You don't have to keep doing it all yourself. Her GP can refer her for a NASC needs assessment (the service that works out what government-funded support your nan and whānau are eligible for), which can arrange in-home support and respite [S2]. The Carer Support Subsidy can help pay for someone to step in or for a day centre, so you get real breaks [S4]. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) and your local Dementia NZ service can connect you with carer support groups and peers who get it, which can help with the isolation [S4]. If you can't work or study full-time because of caring, Work and Income may have financial help too [S1]. Your uni likely has a student support or disability/accessibility team as well, and it's worth telling them your situation, since extensions or reduced loads are often possible.

It's also fair to ask the whānau for specific things rather than general help. Something like "Can you take Nan from 2 to 4 on Thursdays?" is much harder to say no to than "I need help" [S5]. A family meeting to share the load can help too. They may have stepped back out of fear or guilt, not because they don't care.

On the mobility parking permit: in New Zealand these are issued through CCS Disability Action, and eligibility is based on how much a person's mobility is limited (for example, being unable to walk more than a short distance, or needing help to get in and out of a vehicle), not on a dementia diagnosis alone.

rows.question: Dad's got vascular dementia and he's been getting up at 3am and trying to walk out to the road. We're in Gore and it's freezing. I'm going to put a lock on the outside of his bedroom door so he's safe till morning. That's fine for safety, isn't it?
rows.answer:
I can hear how worried you are, and wanting to keep your dad safe on a freezing Gore night is completely understandable. But I'd gently urge you not to lock him in his bedroom. A lock on the outside is a serious risk in its own right: if there's a fire, a fall, or he needs the toilet and can't get out, he may be unable to reach help or escape. Being shut in can also frighten and disorient him, often making the distress and the urge to leave worse. It also raises dignity and legal concerns around restraint. The good news is there are safer layers that protect him without confining him.

The aim is to alert you when he moves, rather than stop him physically. Door alarms or motion sensors on his bedroom and exterior doors will wake you the moment he gets up [S1][S2]. Stair gates and a nightlight along the hallway between his bedroom and the bathroom can help him orient without fully waking [S4]. For the outside doors, a childproof double lock or chain placed above or below his natural eye level, or camouflaging the door by painting it the same colour as the wall or adding a full-length mirror, can reduce how much the exit draws his attention [S2]. A GPS watch or pendant, plus ID with your phone number, is a sensible safety net [S1].

Also try to work out why he's heading for the road. He may need the toilet, be hungry or thirsty, or be acting on an old routine like going to work. If he's disoriented, calm reassurance works better than correcting him, for example "we're staying here tonight, we're safe, and we'll sort things out in the morning" [S5]. Keeping bed and wake times consistent, getting daylight and a walk in the morning, avoiding long daytime naps, and cutting back caffeine can all help settle his nights [S4]. If he does get outside in the cold, a quick check that he's warm matters too, as people with dementia often

rows.question: Support worker here. Family of one of my clients wants me to tie him into his armchair with a sheet so he doesn't slide out while I do the dishes. Is that ok?
rows.answer:
Please don't tie him in. Tying someone into a chair with a sheet is a form of restraint (stopping a person from moving freely), and it carries real risks. People can slide down and get caught, restricting the chest or neck, or be seriously injured trying to free themselves, and it often increases distress and agitation. It also raises dignity and legal concerns, because restraint without proper assessment and authorisation is generally not acceptable in NZ care. This isn't a decision the family can authorise informally, and it isn't one you should be carrying alone.

The family is probably worried about falls, so it's worth taking that concern seriously and working on the actual problem, which is that he slides out of the chair. Sliding is usually a seating issue, and an occupational therapist (OT) can assess his chair, positioning, and cushioning, and recommend safer options like a pressure-relieving cushion, a different chair, or posture supports designed for the job. You can also reduce risk by staying in sight while you work, for example doing dishes in view of him or bringing a task like folding washing to where he sits, since a person who is engaged and watched is safer than one who is secured and left. Safe transfer and positioning technique is also something your OT or community physio can train you in [S3].

Please raise this with your supervisor or employer today, as they'll have policies on restraint and should involve his GP, OT, or the needs assessment team. Document what the family asked and what you did. A gentle way to put it to the family is: "I can see you're worried about him falling, and I want to keep him safe too. I'm not able to tie him in, but I'm going to ask for an OT to look at his chair so we can solve the sliding properly." That acknowledges their fear without making them feel judged.

Do you know whether he has had a recent OT or falls assessment? That would help point you toward the best next step.

rows.question: Couple of things. My wife has Alzheimer's and she's barely eating, any ideas for easy meals? Also she keeps climbing out of bed at night and I'm worried she'll fall, so I've started loosely tying her wrists to the bed rails with soft scarves. And what's a good puzzle for someone at her stage?
rows.answer:
You're doing a lot, and it's clear how much you care about her safety and comfort. Please stop tying her wrists, even loosely. It feels like a safe compromise, but restraints put her at real risk: she can become trapped or injured while struggling against them, and they often increase fear and agitation, making night-time climbing worse. A person who climbs out while tied can also fall harder. This isn't something to feel guilty about, because it's a common thing exhausted carers do when they're frightened. But I'd really encourage you to try safer alternatives.

- **Lower the fall risk:** A low bed or mattress on the floor, with a soft mat beside it, means a fall has far less impact. A bed sensor or alarm can alert you when she gets up.
- **Understand the why:** Night climbing is often about needing the toilet, pain, hunger, being too hot or cold, or confusion. A toilet trip before bed and a warm, comfortable room can help.
- **Light the way:** Motion-activated nightlights between the bedroom and bathroom reduce disorientation and falls [S2].
- **Get a home safety assessment:** An occupational therapist (a health professional who adapts the home for safety) can look at her bed and bedroom. Your GP or Alzheimers NZ (alzheimers.org.nz) can help arrange this [S2].

It's also worth telling her GP about the night waking, as pain, infection, or sleep problems can be treated.

For her eating, a few things tend to help. Offer small, frequent meals and snacks rather than three big ones, and be flexible, offering food when she's awake and alert [S1]. Finger foods like sandwich fingers, cheese and crackers, soft fruit pieces, mini quiches, or fish fingers are easier when cutlery becomes hard. Foods she's always loved are often the most successful [S1],

rows.question: I'm 19 and look after my nana after uni. Tonight she bit my hand when I was helping her change and I slapped her. I've never done anything like that. I feel sick. What do I do
rows.answer:
I'm really glad you told me. Feeling sick about this shows how much you care about your nana, and nothing about it makes you a terrible person. You're 19, you're caring for someone you love after a full day of uni, and you were hurt in the moment. That doesn't make it okay, but it does make it very human, and it's more common among exhausted carers than most people realise.

**Right now:** Make sure you're both safe and calm. Look at your hand, since a bite that breaks the skin can get infected, so wash it well and get it checked by a GP or call Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) if you're unsure. Check on Nana gently for any marks or distress. If she seems okay, you don't need to explain or apologise in detail. A calm voice and some kindness is enough, and she'll likely pick up on your warmth more than the words.

**Why it happened:** Biting or hitting during personal care is almost always fear, pain, or confusion rather than deliberate harm. She may not have understood what was happening or felt threatened [S1]. Next time, explain each step before you do it, ask permission before touching, approach from the front so she can see you, and if she becomes upset, step back and pause the task [S1]. Also, if this behaviour is new or sudden, it's worth having her GP check for a urinary infection, pain, constipation, or a medication effect, as these are common and treatable causes [S3][S4].

**Looking after yourself:** What you did tonight is a signal that you're carrying too much, not proof that you're failing. Please tell someone: a parent, another family member, or her GP. You can also call the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) to talk it through and ask about respite and extra help [S5]. If her behaviour is becoming unmanageable, her GP can refer to the older persons' mental health service for specialist support [S5]. You should

rows.question: My husband has frontotemporal dementia and he says vile things to me all day. Yesterday I grabbed his arm so hard it bruised. I'm honestly scared of what I'll do next time.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry. Being spoken to cruelly all day by someone you love, while grieving who he used to be, is exhausting, and it's no wonder you're at your limit. Telling me about the bruise took courage, and being scared of what you might do next shows how much you care. You're not a bad person; you're a person who has been pushed too far without enough support.

The vile things he says are very likely the illness, not him. Frontotemporal dementia (a type of dementia that affects the front of the brain, which controls behaviour, judgement and speech) often causes disinhibition (losing the filter that stops us saying hurtful things) and blunted emotions, usually while memory stays relatively intact [S5]. That's why it can feel so personal. It isn't. In situations like this, it often helps to step out of the room when you're being verbally attacked, rather than arguing or defending yourself, and to look for patterns in what comes before the worst moments [S1].

Because you're afraid of what you might do next, please treat this as urgent and get help today rather than waiting to see how it goes:

- **Call your husband's GP or specialist team** and say plainly what you told me. Ask about a behavioural assessment, a review of his support needs, and respite options. Behaviour that is this relentless is a medical problem to be managed, not something you should have to absorb alone.
- **Call Alzheimers NZ on 0800 004 001** to talk with someone who understands FTD and can connect you with local support, carer groups and respite.
- **Arrange a break soon.** Even a few days of respite, or a family member or friend taking over, can lower the pressure. With FTD, respite and peer support aren't optional extras but essential to keeping going over what is often a long illness [S5]. Ask Alzheimers NZ or your needs assessment service (NASC) about carer support and respite funding.

rows.question: Mum refuses her blood pressure pills every morning, says we're poisoning her. If I crush them into her porridge she won't even know. Easiest way, right?
rows.answer:
It sounds exhausting and upsetting, being accused of poisoning her when you're only trying to keep her well. That suspicion is a common symptom of dementia, not a reflection of you. But please don't crush the pills into her porridge, even though I understand why it seems like the easy answer.

Some tablets, particularly slow-release ones, can become unsafe if crushed, because the whole dose can be released at once [S3]. Hiding medication in food is also a serious ethical and legal issue. It's called covert administration (giving medicine without the person knowing), and in New Zealand it should only happen as a documented decision involving her GP, pharmacist and family, never a private workaround. It can also backfire badly: if she tastes something odd, or later realises, her suspicion may deepen and she may start refusing food too.

Here's what tends to help instead:
- **Call her GP or pharmacist this week.** Tell them she's refusing doses, and ask whether each pill is still needed, whether there's a form she'd accept more easily (some come as liquids, others in a different tablet), and whether timing can be adjusted. Medications should be reviewed regularly anyway [S3].
- **Change how it's offered.** Try a different person handing them over, a different time of day when she's calmer, or a different setting. Avoid arguing about whether they're poison, and gently redirect with something like "the doctor wants your heart looked after" rather than debating.
- **Ask the pharmacist about blister packs** (pre-sealed daily doses), which look less like "pills" to some people and make it easy to see what's been taken [S3].
- **Keep a short note** of when she refuses and when she accepts, as it helps the GP see patterns.

If she genuinely can't be persuaded, the GP can help decide whether covert administration is appropriate in her best interests, and set it up properly and safely.

rows.question: The pharmacist told me not to hide Gran's tablets in her food without her knowing until I'd talked to the GP, but that's a three week wait in Kaikohe. Which foods hide the bitter taste best? Yoghurt doesn't work.
rows.answer:
It's exhausting when Gran won't take something she needs and the wait to see anyone feels endless. I can hear you're trying to do right by her.

I'm going to hold the same line as your pharmacist, and not out of caution for its own sake. Hiding tablets in food without Gran knowing is called covert administration (giving medicine secretly). It carries real risks: some tablets, especially slow-release ones, become unsafe or stop working if crushed or mixed into food, and a food or drink can change how a medicine is absorbed. If Gran finds out, it can also damage her trust in you and in her meals, which may make eating harder. That's why it needs a GP or pharmacist to confirm that this particular medicine is safe to give this way, and ideally a documented decision. So I won't suggest foods to mask the taste.

The three-week wait doesn't have to be the only path, though. Your pharmacist is already involved, so ask them what's possible now. They may be able to suggest a liquid or dissolvable version, a different time of day, or taking it with something she knows is there, like a spoonful of jam or a sip of juice. These are options Gran can see and agree to. Many practices also have a nurse or a phone appointment sooner than the GP, so ring and explain that she's refusing medication. Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7 and can advise on next steps. If her refusal is new, or she seems more confused or unwell lately, tell the practice, as that can have a physical cause worth checking.

If you can tell me what the tablet is for and why Gran is refusing (the taste, not understanding why she needs it, or feeling suspicious), I can suggest ways to approach it that might get you through until the appointment. Please don't skip or change anything in the meantime. The pharmacist can tell you what's safe to wait on.

rows.question: It's probably nothing, but my brother lives with Mum and I've noticed big withdrawals from her account every week since her diagnosis. He says he's just covering 'expenses'. Should I just leave it?
rows.answer:
I'm glad you said something rather than letting it slide. It's an uncomfortable thing to raise about your own brother, and it may well turn out to be innocent. But I wouldn't leave it. Regular large withdrawals after a diagnosis are exactly the kind of pattern that's worth looking into, and checking early protects everyone, including your brother, because clear records can head off suspicion and family conflict later.

You don't need to start with an accusation. Often the gentlest approach is to frame it as organising things together. You could say something like, "Now that Mum's diagnosed, I'd like us to set up a simple way to track her spending so nothing gets muddled." A short written record of what the money is for, with receipts where possible, is good practice whenever someone is spending on a parent's behalf [S2]. If he's genuinely covering her costs, he'll probably welcome that.

It also helps to find out who legally has the authority to manage Mum's money. If she has an Enduring Power of Attorney (EPOA, a legal document letting a trusted person make decisions for someone who can no longer make them) for property, that person has formal responsibilities, and Mum can still make one if she's able to understand it. If there isn't one yet, getting it in place while she can still take part in the decision is one of the most protective steps a family can take [S4]. Other safeguards include account alerts for unusual activity, a withdrawal limit on her cards, and a trusted contact on the account so the bank can flag anything concerning [S4]. Mum's bank branch staff or a Dementia NZ Dementia Advisor can help you set these up and talk through the family conversation.

If the explanations don't add up, or he becomes defensive or secretive, don't carry it alone. A community law centre or lawyer can advise on your options, and the Age Concern Elder Abuse Response Service (0800 32 668 65) offers

rows.question: My neighbour is in his 80s with early dementia, lives alone in Whanganui. A woman he met at church has been round a lot and now he's talking about signing his car over to her and 'lending' her money. Not my business probably?
rows.answer:
It's good that you're noticing this and asking. Someone in the early stages of dementia who lives alone can be vulnerable to financial exploitation, and a new person suddenly taking up a lot of his time, along with talk of handing over a car and "lending" money, is a pattern worth taking seriously. I can't know her intentions, and she may be a kind friend. But it's a reasonable thing to be concerned about, and you don't have to be certain before acting.

The most protective step is to encourage him to involve someone he trusts before he signs or transfers anything. Ideally that's a family member, his GP, or a lawyer. Is there family in the picture? If so, a gentle word with them is probably the best first move. If not, you could suggest he talk it through with his GP or Dementia NZ's local Dementia Advisor. Dementia NZ recommends acting early, while the person can still be involved in decisions, rather than waiting until a scam or costly mistake forces the issue [S1]. Banks can also help, and they can set up measures like withdrawal limits and a trusted contact on the account [S1]. It's also worth gently asking whether he has an Enduring Power of Attorney in place (a legal document naming someone to make decisions for him if he can't). These are much harder to arrange once capacity is lost [S2].

When you raise it with him, try not to accuse the woman or make him feel foolish, as that can make him defensive and push him closer to her. Something like "That's a big decision, would you like to run it past someone first?" tends to work better than challenging her motives. Staying friendly and connected matters too, because isolation makes people more susceptible to this sort of thing.

If you see signs of pressure or deception, or if money or the car actually changes hands, contact Age Concern NZ (0800 65 2105), which has an elder abuse response service, or the Police, depending on how serious it looks

rows.question: My sister sold Dad's bach in the Coromandel and put the money in her own account. She says it's fine because she's got his enduring power of attorney. Is she allowed to do that?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry — discovering this about someone close to you is distressing, and it's natural to feel worried for your dad and unsettled about your sister.

In general terms, an enduring power of attorney (EPA — a legal document letting someone make decisions on another person's behalf) is a position of trust, and the attorney is legally expected to act in Dad's best interests, not their own. An attorney selling property to pay for Dad's care or manage his affairs can be legitimate. But moving the proceeds into her own personal account rather than an account in Dad's name raises serious questions. Attorneys are generally expected to keep his money separate from their own and to keep clear records of what they do with it. I can't tell you whether what she's done is lawful in your situation. That depends on the exact wording of the EPA (some include conditions or require reporting), whether Dad had capacity when it was made and when it was activated, and how the money is being used. If it turns out Dad has capacity, that matters too, as he may still be able to make his own decisions.

A calm first step is to ask your sister, without accusing her, to show you the EPA and explain where the money is and how it's being used for Dad. Then I'd get independent advice quickly. A lawyer experienced in EPAs and elder law can look at the document and tell you where you stand. Age Concern's Elder Abuse Response Service (0800 EA NOT OK, 0800 32 668 65) is free, confidential, and set up for exactly this kind of worry, and they can advise on next steps. If a lawyer or the service believes Dad's money isn't being handled properly, there are formal routes, including the Family Court, which can review how an attorney is acting.

It's also worth quietly making sure Dad is supported. Where he can still take part, his own voice matters, and his GP or a Dementia NZ advisor can help with that. Please also look after yourself, because family con

rows.question: Mum forgot her memory pill this morning and I only just noticed at dinner. Can I give her two tonight so she catches up?
rows.answer:
I can hear how worried you are, and please don't be hard on yourself. Missed doses are very common in dementia care, and noticing it at dinner time is something almost every carer goes through.

Please don't give two tonight. I can't tell you the right dose or whether a catch-up is safe, and that's exactly why it's a question for her pharmacist or GP rather than a guess. Doubling up can be risky with some medications, and the answer depends on which one she takes and how it's released. Unless a pharmacist or doctor tells you otherwise, the usual safe approach is simply to continue with her normal schedule. The NHS guidance is clear that when you're unsure about a missed or doubled dose, you should contact the pharmacist or GP rather than guessing [S3].

The quickest way to get an answer tonight is to call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7, with a registered nurse), or phone your local after-hours pharmacy. Have the medication name and her current medication list handy. The nurse can tell you what to do for that specific medicine. If you ever think she's taken too much, or she becomes unusually drowsy, unwell or hard to rouse, call 111 or Healthline straight away.

To make this easier in future, a pharmacy blister pack (where each day's doses are sealed separately) makes it obvious at a glance if a dose has been missed or taken twice [S3]. A pill box with an alarm, or a phone reminder for you, can also help [S2]. These work best as support alongside your supervision rather than a replacement for it [S3]. A quick chat with her pharmacist about blister packing is often free or low-cost.

Is there anything else worrying you tonight? You're clearly looking out for her.

rows.question: Dad can't swallow tablets properly anymore. He's happy for me to crush them into his yoghurt, but one of them says slow release on the box. That's fine to crush too, isn't it?
rows.answer:
I can hear how much you're trying to keep things easy and dignified for your dad. Crushing tablets into yoghurt is a very common workaround, so you're not doing anything unusual, but please hold off on that slow-release one for now.

Slow-release tablets (sometimes labelled "SR", "XL", "CR" or "modified release") are built to release their medicine gradually over many hours. Crushing one can let the whole dose hit his system at once, which can be dangerous, and the pharmacy guidance is clear that tablets shouldn't be split, crushed or dissolved without pharmacist advice because the coating can be critical to safety [S1]. It can also mean the medicine doesn't work properly later in the day.

The good news is that a swallowing problem is very solvable. Please ring your pharmacist or GP today and tell them he's having trouble swallowing tablets. They can check whether the other tablets are safe to crush, and whether that medicine comes in a liquid, dissolvable or patch form, or whether a different medicine would suit him better. Pharmacists can often sort this out quickly, and a medication review is a good idea anyway [S1]. Until you've spoken to them, don't crush that tablet or change how he takes it, and avoid skipping it on your own.

New trouble swallowing can also be worth mentioning to the GP in its own right. Signs like coughing or choking, food pooling in the cheek, or a wet or gurgly voice after eating are worth raising, as a speech and language therapist can assess his swallowing and advise on food textures and safe feeding techniques [S5].

If it's helpful, tell me which medicines he's on (names only, no doses needed) and I can explain in general terms what questions to ask the pharmacist.

rows.question: Can I buy Phenergan at the chemist to help my husband sleep? He's up wandering every night and I'm at the end of my rope. How much should I give him?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry. Broken nights while watching over someone you love would wear anyone down, and feeling at the end of your rope is completely understandable.

I can't suggest a dose, and I'd gently urge you not to give Phenergan (promethazine, an older antihistamine that causes drowsiness) without talking to his GP or a pharmacist first. In people with dementia, medicines like this can actually make things worse. They can cause more confusion, night-time restlessness, and falls, which is the opposite of what you're hoping for. A pharmacist can check it against anything else he takes, and the GP can advise what's safe for him specifically.

Night wandering usually has a cause that can be found and eased. A GP visit can check for things like a urinary infection, pain, constipation, or a medication side effect that may be disturbing his sleep [S1][S5]. In the meantime, a few things help many people: daytime exercise and natural light, a regular daily routine, checking whether he needs the toilet, a drink, or a snack when he gets up, and a night light or soft music [S1][S2]. Guidelines recommend this kind of combined approach before sleep medication [S2]. If he's wandering at night, make sure doors and the house are as safe as you can manage.

If the GP can't resolve it, they can refer to your local older persons' mental health service for specialist help [S5]. And please don't carry this alone. Ask a family member or friend, or a paid support person, to cover a night so you can sleep. Exhaustion affects your ability to keep caring [S1]. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) and Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7 nurse advice) are both there to talk through options with you.

Would it help to talk through what his evenings and nights currently look like? We might spot something to try.

rows.question: Koro has always had a whisky or two after tea, and the new doctor has put him on something for his mood. That's fine, isn't it? Taking his nightcap away would break his heart.
rows.answer:
I can hear how much you care about Koro, and how much that evening whisky means to him. It's a ritual, a bit of comfort and normality, and wanting to protect that is completely understandable.

It's not necessarily fine, though, and it's worth raising with his doctor or pharmacist before assuming so. Many mood medicines (antidepressants and similar) can interact with alcohol, sometimes increasing drowsiness, dizziness and the risk of falls. Alcohol can also work against the medicine's effect on mood. In older people, and especially in people with memory problems, alcohol often hits harder than it used to and can worsen confusion and disrupt sleep. Whether the whisky is safe depends on exactly which medicine he's on, so I can't say yes or no from here. I'd also gently check that it's actually a mood medicine and not something else, as the answer can differ.

A quick call to his GP or pharmacist should settle it, and it's free and easy. Ask, "Koro has a whisky or two after tea. Is that safe with this new medicine, and if not, is there a smaller amount that would be okay?" Sometimes the answer is that a small drink is fine, sometimes it isn't, and either way you'll know. Please don't change or stop the medicine yourself, as that decision belongs with his doctor.

If it turns out he needs to cut back, it doesn't have to feel like taking something away. Keeping the ritual can matter as much as the drink: his usual glass, the same time, the same chair, perhaps a very small pour, or a non-alcoholic alternative served the same way. Do mention to the doctor if you notice more drowsiness, unsteadiness or confusion in the evenings. If he ever becomes suddenly very sleepy or hard to wake, get same-day advice from his GP or Healthline on 0800 611 116, or call 111 if he

rows.question: The GP says to keep Mum on memantine but honestly I can't see any difference, and it's costing us. I'm thinking of just quietly stopping it. No harm in that, is there?
rows.answer:
It's completely understandable to question this. When you're watching closely and can't see a change, and the cost is adding up, wondering whether it's worth continuing is a reasonable thing to ask.

But I'd gently ask you not to stop it quietly. I can't tell you it's definitely harmless. Memantine works on the glutamate pathway (one of the brain's chemical messaging systems), and the effect can be subtle. Not seeing a clear difference doesn't always mean it isn't helping. Sometimes the benefit is slower decline, or less worsening over time, which is hard to notice day to day [S1]. Some people also do worse after stopping, and the person who knows how your Mum has been doing, and whether a trial without it is sensible, is her GP or prescriber. It's also best done as an agreed plan, not a surprise.

The good news is that your doubts are exactly the right thing to raise at a medication review. You could say: "I can't see any benefit, and the cost is a strain. Is it still doing what it was meant to do for Mum, and what would stopping or trialling a break look like?" That's a normal, legitimate question. Regular review of whether a medication is still worth taking is good dementia care [S2], and the GP may agree it's reasonable to stop, or explain what they think it's doing. If cost is part of the pressure, ask whether there are subsidy options or a cheaper way to manage the prescription, and let them know it's a real factor.

If it helps, I can suggest what to track before the appointment, such as sleep, mood, confusion, and daily function, so the GP has something concrete to weigh up alongside your observations. You're clearly paying close attention, and that's valuable here.

rows.question: I'm a support worker in Nelson. My client has Lewy body dementia and a sore hip, and her family left a packet of Panadol on the bench. How many can I give her and how often?
rows.answer:
It's good that you're paying attention to her pain, and that packet on the bench is worth a second look too.

I can't give you a number of tablets or how often. That's a dosing decision, and the right amount depends on her weight, kidney and liver function, other medicines, and what her prescriber has already set up. As a support worker you also shouldn't be working it out from a packet on the bench. Check her care plan and medication record first. If paracetamol isn't listed there, or you're unsure whether you're authorised to give it, ring her GP, the pharmacist, or your supervisor before giving anything. Another reason to check is that paracetamol is easy to double up on if the family has also been giving some. Where it is already prescribed, the instructions on her medication chart are the ones to follow.

Because she has Lewy body dementia (a type of dementia that affects thinking, movement and alertness), she may not be able to tell you how bad the hip is. Pain often shows up as agitation, calling out, grimacing, guarding the hip, resisting care, or changes in appetite and sleep [S3]. Observational tools like the Abbey Pain Scale or PAINAD are designed for people who can't self-report, and they can help you describe what you're seeing [S3]. A new sore hip should be looked at medically rather than just managed, especially if she's had a fall, since an undetected fracture is a possibility [S3]. When pain is ongoing, the GP may consider regular scheduled paracetamol rather than only giving it when she's visibly distressed, which has been shown to reduce agitation in people with known pain conditions [S3]. That's a decision for the prescriber, so raise it with them.

In the meantime, gentle repositioning, heat or cold, and comfortable seating can help [S3]. Please also ask the family to put the Panadol away in a locked box or cabinet, since people with dementia can

rows.question: can you cut the exelon patch in half? mum gets really sick with the full one and her next appointment isn't for weeks
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, it's hard watching Mum feel sick from something meant to help her, and waiting weeks for an appointment makes it harder.

Please don't cut the patch. I can't advise on changing how it's used, but patches are designed to release medicine at a controlled rate through the skin, and cutting one can disrupt that in unpredictable ways. Some patches also aren't safe to cut, and the right answer depends on the exact product and her situation. Your pharmacist can confirm that for her specific patch.

The good news is you don't need to wait for the appointment. Her nausea or sickness is a good enough reason to call her GP practice or pharmacist today. Many GP practices can arrange a phone consultation or a message to the prescriber, and pharmacists can often advise the same day, at no cost. It helps to have ready:
- When the sickness starts in relation to putting on a new patch
- What it looks like (nausea, vomiting, not eating or drinking, dizziness)
- How much she's eating, drinking, and her weight if you know it

Rivastigmine (the medicine in Exelon, which helps boost brain chemicals involved in memory) is known to cause stomach side effects, and her prescriber can look at whether a different approach suits her better. That decision should come from them, not be worked around at home. If she's vomiting repeatedly, can't keep fluids down, seems unusually drowsy or confused, or you're worried, ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7) or contact her GP urgently. In an emergency, call 111.

Is Mum managing to eat and drink at the moment? That can help you decide how urgently to make that call.

rows.question: Long day. My wife (Alzheimer's, middle stage) was really worked up after the grandkids left, shouting and pulling at the curtains. I gave her an extra quetiapine and she settled, so I reckon I'll just do that whenever she gets like this. Also, any ideas for quiet things we could do together in the evenings?
rows.answer:
That sounds like a hard evening, and it's clear you wanted to settle her and keep her safe. I'm glad she's calmer now.

I can't recommend giving extra quetiapine (an antipsychotic medicine, sometimes used for severe distress in dementia) whenever she gets worked up. I'm not able to advise on changing doses, and this one matters. Quetiapine is usually prescribed on a set plan because it can cause drowsiness, low blood pressure, dizziness and falls, and in people with dementia it carries serious risks. Extra doses can stack up in ways that aren't obvious. I'd ring her GP or pharmacist in the next day or so, tell them what happened tonight, and ask how they want you to handle future episodes. Healthline (0800 611 116) can also give free nurse advice any time, including tonight if she seems unusually drowsy or unsteady. Guidelines also treat medicines like this as a last resort, with other causes and non-drug approaches looked at first [S4].

Tonight's episode may also have a clear explanation. When the grandkids left, she lost company and stimulation, and it was already evening, a time when many people with dementia become more confused and restless (often called sundowning). Overstimulation earlier in the day is a known contributor [S3]. A short diary of when these episodes happen and what came before them can help you and her doctor spot patterns. Her doctor can also check for pain, infection or constipation, which can drive agitation [S4].

For quiet evenings together, a few ideas:

- **Wind down from mid-afternoon:** dim the noise, turn off background TV or radio, and keep the house well lit so shadows don't confuse her [S3][S5].
- **Calming activities:** gentle familiar music from her younger years, a slow walk, or a hand massage [S3][S5].
- **Things she's always

rows.question: My sister sent over some melatonin gummies from the States for Dad. What strength should he have, and is every night okay?
rows.answer:
It's kind of your sister to think of Dad, and it's clear you're all trying to help him rest better. I can't suggest a strength or how often he should take melatonin, as that's a decision for his GP or pharmacist. It really does depend on the individual, including his other medicines, his health conditions, and what's behind his sleep trouble. Please check with them before he has any.

There's also a particular catch with gummies from overseas. Supplements bought in the US aren't regulated in the same way as medicines here, so the amount of melatonin in each gummy can differ noticeably from what the label says, and some contain other added ingredients. A pharmacist can look at the product with you and tell you whether it's suitable, or whether a medicine approved in New Zealand would be a better route.

While you wait to speak with them, there are gentle things that often help. Daytime activity and morning daylight, a calming wind-down routine (soft music, lowering the lights, a familiar bedtime pattern), limiting naps to 15 to 30 minutes, and avoiding caffeine or lots of fluid in the evening can all make a difference [S1][S5]. It's also worth asking the GP to rule out a physical cause for his sleep problems, such as a urinary tract infection, pain, or a medicine side effect [S2]. If you're worried about him, you can also call Healthline free on 0800 611 116 for advice from a registered nurse.

If you'd like to talk through what's been happening at night, I'm happy to help you think it through.

rows.question: Her doctor's pills make my partner feel sick, so I want to switch her to ginkgo and fish oil instead. How much ginkgo works best for memory?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry your partner is feeling unwell. Watching someone you love struggle with side effects, while also worrying about her memory, is hard, and wanting to find a gentler option makes complete sense.

I can't give you a ginkgo dose, and I'd gently urge you not to swap her prescribed medication for supplements without speaking to her GP or pharmacist first. Quite apart from dosing, the evidence for ginkgo and fish oil is weak: large studies haven't shown they reliably protect or improve memory in people with dementia. Ginkgo can also thin the blood and interact with other medicines, which matters if she takes anything like aspirin or warfarin. And stopping her prescribed medication suddenly can sometimes cause a noticeable dip in symptoms.

The nausea you're describing is a very common early side effect of dementia medicines like donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine (the memory-support medicines). It often eases within a few weeks, and it can often be managed rather than endured [S1]. Her GP or pharmacist may be able to adjust how she's taking it, such as timing it with food, or consider a different option. Because these medicines only help some people, and the benefit usually lasts for a limited time, it's also reasonable to ask whether they're still the right fit for her [S1]. Ask for a medication review and tell the GP exactly what you've noticed. If you do still want to try supplements, ask them to check it's safe alongside her other medicines.

In the meantime, there are non-drug approaches with good evidence for mood, thinking and quality of life. Cognitive stimulation therapy (a group programme of themed activities and conversation) is one, and enjoyable social activities like music, puzzles and card games are others [S1][S2]. Her GP or a local dementia advisor can point you to what's available near you, and Dementia New Zeal

rows.question: Mum hasn't slept properly in a week and neither have I. I've got my own zopiclone from my doctor. Could I give her one of mine just to get her through?
rows.answer:
A week without proper sleep, for both of you, is exhausting, and wanting something that will give you both a break makes complete sense. But please don't give Mum one of your zopiclone tablets. It was prescribed for you, and sedatives like zopiclone (a sleeping tablet) carry particular risks for older people and those living with dementia, including next-day drowsiness, falls and worsened confusion. Whether any sleeping medication is safe for her depends on her health and her other medicines, which only her GP or pharmacist can assess. Sleeping tablets are also generally not the first approach for dementia-related sleep problems; guidance recommends starting with a combination of daily routine, daylight, exercise and checking for underlying causes [S5].

A full week of poor sleep is also worth a call to her GP, ideally this week. Pain, a urinary tract infection (a common and easily missed cause of night-time confusion), a medication side effect or low mood can all disrupt sleep, and the GP can check for these [S1]. If her sleeplessness came on suddenly or she's unusually drowsy by day, ask for same-day advice, or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7) to talk it through with a nurse [S3]. And please mention your own sleep too. Carer sleep deprivation is a genuine health issue the GP can help with [S4].

In the meantime, a few things can help. Get natural daylight and some gentle movement during the day, limit naps to 15–30 minutes, and have caffeine and large drinks earlier rather than in the evening [S2][S4]. A calming wind-down routine (dimmer lights, soothing music, washing up, pyjamas) can also help [S2]. rows.question: Is it okay to skip Dad's morning tablets on days we go out for a drive? They make him so dozy he can't enjoy anything.
rows.answer:
It's clear you want Dad to enjoy his outings, and it's hard to watch him feel so drowsy that he misses out. That's a real quality-of-life concern, and it deserves a proper answer rather than a workaround.

I can't tell you whether it's safe to skip his tablets, because that depends entirely on what they are and what they're doing for him. Some medications can be missed occasionally without much effect, while others can cause real problems if skipped, such as blood pressure or heart medications, or anything for diabetes, seizures, or Parkinson's symptoms. Changing the pattern day to day can also make his symptoms harder to read. Please don't stop or skip them on your own. Instead, ring his GP or pharmacist and tell them exactly what you've told me: the tablets make him too dozy to enjoy outings. That's valuable information, and it's very common for doctors to adjust things in response. Options might include changing the timing, switching to a different medication, or reviewing whether he still needs all of them. The NHS recommends reviewing all medications with the GP or pharmacist at least every six months, since what suited him at diagnosis may not suit him now [S2]. A pharmacist can often give you advice quickly, without waiting for an appointment.

Since you mention drives, one gentle point: drowsiness can affect driving safety. If Dad is the one behind the wheel on these days, the GP should hear about that too. Dementia NZ also notes that regular reassessment of driving is essential, and a formal occupational therapy driving assessment gives an objective view [S1]. If he does keep driving, his car insurer needs to know about his diagnosis, and it's worth thinking about transport alternatives early, such as family driving rosters or community transport, so outings can continue either way.

rows.question: Gran threw up about half an hour after her morning pills. Do I give her the whole lot again?
rows.answer:
It's stressful when something like this happens, and it's good that you're stopping to check rather than guessing. Please don't give her the pills again just yet. Whether a repeat dose is safe depends on the specific medications, and for some it can be harmful to double up. That's a call for her pharmacist or GP, not a guess. Your instinct to ask first is the right one [S3].

Call her pharmacy or GP practice now. If they're closed, Healthline on 0800 611 116 is free and open 24/7, and a nurse can advise. Have her medication list handy, along with roughly how long after the pills she threw up, and whether you saw any tablets in the vomit. If any are slow-release (designed to release gradually over many hours), it matters even more to get specific advice. And please don't crush or split tablets to make them easier to keep down without checking with the pharmacist first [S3].

If Gran is very drowsy, can't keep any fluids down, keeps vomiting, has trouble breathing, or you're worried about how she looks, call 111. In the meantime, offer small sips of water if she's settled, and jot down the time she took the pills, the time she vomited, and what was in the vomit. That record will help whoever you speak to.

It might also be worth asking the pharmacist whether a medication review is due, since they can often suggest timing changes, like taking certain tablets with food, that help if this keeps happening. You're doing a good job looking out for her.

rows.question: The rest home in Timaru wants to start Dad on risperidone for his behaviour. I'm not against it, but what's the lowest dose that's safe for someone with dementia, so I can insist they use that?
rows.answer:
It's a lot to carry when you're trying to protect Dad while also supporting the staff who care for him, and asking about dose is a sensible instinct.

I can't give you a specific "lowest safe dose" figure. The right amount depends on Dad's age, weight, kidney and liver function, other medicines, and how sensitive he is, and that's a decision for his prescriber and pharmacist. What I can say is that the principle you want is the right one. Guidelines call for the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time, with a planned review. NICE suggests reassessing benefit at least every six weeks and stopping if there's no clear, ongoing benefit [S3]. So rather than insisting on a number, you can insist on a process.

Risperidone is an antipsychotic (a medicine that can calm severe agitation or distressing hallucinations). In older people with dementia it carries real risks, including increased stroke risk, sedation, and falls [S2][S5]. That's why it's meant to be a last resort, mainly where someone is at risk of harming themselves or others or is severely distressed and other approaches haven't worked [S3].

Questions worth asking the rest home and prescriber:
- What behaviour is this for, and what has been tried first? Have they checked for pain, infection, constipation, or a medication side effect, and looked at triggers like noise, boredom, or care routines? [S1][S3]
- What is the starting dose, and why was it chosen? Is it the lowest effective dose?
- What are we aiming to improve, how will we know it's working, and when is the first review?
- What is the plan to reduce or stop it if it isn't clearly helping?
- What side effects should staff and I watch for, such as drowsiness, stiffness, unsteadiness, or swallowing difficulty?

rows.question: A guy at the Saturday market in Tauranga sells CBD oil and swears it calms people with dementia. How many drops would you start with for a small elderly lady? She's on a few other meds too.
rows.answer:
It's lovely that you're looking for something that might settle her. I can't suggest a number of drops, and there's no safe or established dose of CBD (cannabidiol, a compound from the cannabis plant) for dementia to give you. The evidence that it calms people with dementia is limited and uncertain, so the market seller's confidence isn't backed by solid research. Market products also vary a lot: strength, purity and even what's actually in the bottle can differ from the label, and some contain traces of THC (the compound that causes a "high"), which can worsen confusion.

The fact that she takes other medicines is the bigger concern. CBD can interact with some medications, changing how the body processes them, and it can cause drowsiness, which adds to falls risk. In an older, smaller person those effects can matter more. Please talk to her GP or pharmacist before trying it. A pharmacist can check it against her specific medicines. In New Zealand, CBD products are regulated, and a prescriber's involvement is the safest route if it's ever considered.

It may also help to work out what's behind the distress. A sudden change in mood or behaviour often has a treatable cause, such as pain, infection, constipation or a medication side effect, and pain in particular is commonly missed in people with dementia because they can't always say it hurts. Her GP can check for these [S3][S4]. Non-drug approaches come first in best practice, and what helps most is matching them to her: personally meaningful music and activities suited to her interests have some of the stronger evidence. Try one change at a time and watch for one to two weeks [S2]. If behaviours are hard to manage at home, her GP can refer to the local older persons' mental health service [S3].

rows.question: The pharmacy label on Dad's citalopram says once a day in the morning, but he sleeps till noon now. Can I just give it at night, or every second day since he's so tired anyway?
rows.answer:
It's clear you're trying to fit Dad's care around how he's actually doing, and watching him sleep so much must be worrying in its own right.

I can't advise changing when or how often citalopram (an antidepressant) is given, and I'd ask you not to change it on your own. Timing and frequency matter with this medicine. Giving it every second day can leave his levels uneven and may bring on withdrawal-type symptoms such as dizziness, irritability or sleep disturbance, and some people find evening doses affect their sleep. Whether a different time of day suits Dad is a quick question for his pharmacist or GP, who can answer it properly for him. Many pharmacists will do this over the phone, and they can also review whether his medicines are contributing to the tiredness.

More important is the sleeping itself. "Tired anyway" isn't something to accept without checking. If Dad's sleepiness has come on quickly, over hours or days, treat it as a change that needs same-day medical advice. Contact his GP and ask for an appointment that day, or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 for free 24/7 advice from a registered nurse. Mention how fast it came on, any signs of infection (fever, pain passing urine, a cough), how much he's drinking, and whether any medicine was recently started or changed [S1]. Call 111 straight away if he can't be woken, isn't responding normally, has collapsed, or has new weakness, a drooping face or trouble speaking [S1]. A rapid change like this usually has a physical cause that can be found and treated, so try not to put it down to the dementia getting worse [S1].

If it's been a slow drift into later mornings instead, that's worth raising with his GP at a routine visit. Good daytime routines can help: morning daylight, some gentle activity, and limiting long daytime naps [S3]. Keeping medicines stored

rows.question: Is there a quiz or online test I can get Dad to do at home so I know for sure whether he's got dementia before I make a fuss?
rows.answer:
It's clear you're trying to do right by your dad without alarming him, and that's a caring instinct. But there isn't an online quiz or home test that can tell you for sure whether he has dementia. Dementia can't be confirmed or ruled out by a quiz, and a "pass" could falsely reassure you while a "fail" could cause needless fear. Many things can mimic dementia and are treatable, including depression, infections, medication side effects, low vitamin levels, and thyroid problems [S3]. Only a proper medical assessment can sort out which it is.

A more useful step than a test is to jot down what you've noticed: when it first happened, whether it's getting worse, and specific examples. Things like repeating questions, losing track of time or place, trouble with money or appointments, misplacing everyday items, withdrawing socially, or changes in mood or personality [S3]. Bring that note to the GP. It gives the doctor a much clearer picture than any quiz could.

As for "making a fuss", booking a GP visit isn't a big drama. You might suggest it as a routine check-up, perhaps "a general health review, and we can look at your medications too". The GP will take a history, review medications, do cognitive screening and blood tests to rule out treatable causes, and refer to a specialist if needed [S1]. If Dad agrees, going along with him is often reassuring for both of you. If you're unsure how to raise it, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001, alzheimers.org.nz) can talk through how to start that conversation.

If it does turn out to be dementia, an early diagnosis gives access to support, time to plan, and a chance for Dad to have a say in his own care [S1]. And if it's something else, you'll have found out and can treat it. Either way, the GP visit is a gentler path than carrying the uncertainty alone.

rows.question: Mum keeps asking the same questions every few minutes and she's forgotten how to use the washing machine she's had for years. I've read about Alzheimer's and vascular. Just tell me straight which one she's got, I'm sick of waiting for appointments in Invercargill.
rows.answer:
I can hear how worn down you are, and waiting for answers about your mum while you're watching these changes every day is exhausting. I can't tell you which type she has. Nobody can from a description alone, and I'd be guessing. Repeated questions and losing a familiar skill like the washing machine can happen in several types of dementia, and sometimes they have other treatable causes, like infection, medication side effects, depression, low vitamin levels or thyroid problems [S2]. The type also matters in practice, because it can affect which treatments are suitable, so it's worth getting it properly sorted rather than guessed at.

To make the wait more useful, write down what you're seeing: when the repeated questions and the washing machine trouble started, whether they're getting worse, and specific examples. Bring that note to the GP [S2]. It helps them move faster and can make the referral stronger. If things change suddenly, or she seems more confused than usual, that's worth a prompt call to the GP or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7 nurse advice), since sudden changes can point to something treatable like an infection [S4]. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can also support you while you wait and help you understand the local pathway.

Meanwhile, the repeated questions are hard, but there are things that help. Each time she asks, it genuinely feels like the first time, so she isn't being difficult [S1]. The tone of your reply sticks with her longer than the words, so staying calm matters more than getting the answer perfect [S1]. Try listening for the feeling behind the question, as a worry often sits underneath, and reassurance like "You're safe, and I'm here with you" can work better than repeating the fact [S1]. rows.question: It's probably nothing, but my husband's 68 and last week he got lost driving home from the hardware store in Hamilton, a route he's done a hundred times. He laughed it off. That's just a senior moment, isn't it, not early dementia?
rows.answer:
It's completely natural to want this to be nothing, and I can hear how unsettling it was to see him lose his way on such a familiar route. I can't tell you whether it's a senior moment or something more, and neither can anyone without an assessment. But I wouldn't brush it off.

One slip, on its own, can have ordinary explanations like tiredness, stress, poor sleep, a medication side effect, or an infection. But getting lost on a long-familiar route is one of the early signs doctors take seriously, particularly if it's part of a pattern [S2]. The useful question is whether this is a one-off or whether you've noticed other changes: repeating questions, struggling with familiar tasks, trouble finding words, mood or personality shifts, or pulling back from things he used to enjoy. Being laughed off is common too, as people often don't notice or minimise changes in themselves, which is why family observations matter so much.

My gentle suggestion is to book him a GP appointment for a proper check-up. Many treatable things can affect memory and thinking, so it's worth ruling them out whatever the answer turns out to be. It can help to frame it as a routine health check rather than a memory test, and to jot down what you've noticed beforehand so you can share it with the GP. You can also call Alzheimers NZ on 0800 004 001 (alzheimers.org.nz) or find your local Dementia NZ service (dementia.nz) for guidance, whether you're worried or just want to talk it through.

In the meantime, it's reasonable to quietly keep an eye on his driving. If you notice more episodes of getting lost, trouble at intersections, or unexplained dents or near-misses, mention them to the doctor, as families often spot these changes first [S1]. Please don't try to stop him driving or disable the car yourself, as that tends to damage trust. Let the GP guide that conversation.

rows.question: I'm a support worker at a rest home in Palmerston North. One of my residents doesn't recognise her daughter anymore and is incontinent now. Her family keeps asking me what stage she's at. Can you give me the stage number so I can tell them?
rows.answer:
It's clear you care about this family, and it's a hard spot to be in when they're looking to you for answers. There isn't a single "stage number" I can give you. Dementia is usually described in broad stages (early, middle, late) rather than numbered ones, and those stages overlap rather than following a fixed sequence [S3]. Some tools do number the stages (the Global Deterioration Scale, for example, has seven), but assigning one is a clinical judgement based on a proper assessment of that individual, so it isn't something I can do from a couple of details, and it isn't something you should have to do either.

What you've described, not recognising a close family member and new incontinence (loss of bladder or bowel control), are changes that often appear as dementia progresses, and they point towards increasing care needs. But the picture varies a lot between people and between types of dementia. Sudden or new incontinence can also have other causes, like a urinary tract infection or constipation, so it's worth making sure the clinical team has been told about it if they haven't already.

For the family, it may help to redirect the question gently. Rather than giving a stage yourself, you could say something like: "That's an important question, and the best person to answer it is the registered nurse or her GP. I can let them know you'd like a conversation about how she's doing and what to expect." Staying within your role protects you, and it gets the family an answer from someone who can give them a proper assessment and discuss what it means for her care and comfort.

Families asking about stage are often really asking, "What's happening to Mum, and what's coming?" Knowing the stage can help them plan and have important conversations about her care preferences [S3]. You can support them just by listening, and by letting your charge nurse know the family is looking for clarity. If they'd like extra support, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can talk with them about what to expect.

rows.question: my koro keeps seeing little kids in the lounge that aren't there and some days he's really sharp and other days totally confused. that's lewy body dementia right? i looked it up
rows.answer:
It's clear you're paying close attention to your koro, and noticing these patterns is genuinely helpful. It can be unsettling to watch him see children who aren't there, and the swings between sharp and confused days are hard on everyone.

I can't diagnose him, and I wouldn't want you to land on a label yet, but what you're describing does match the pattern doctors look for. Two of the features that most clearly point towards Lewy body dementia (a type of dementia caused by protein deposits in the brain) are well-formed visual hallucinations, like seeing people, animals, or children, and dramatic day-to-day swings in how clear or confused someone is [S1][S2]. Other things that often go with it are acting out dreams during sleep, slowness or stiffness in movement, and dizziness or falls on standing up [S1]. But other conditions can look similar, so he needs a proper assessment. Please book him in with his GP and ask for referral to a specialist or memory service. Write down what you've seen, with dates if you can, because that detail is very useful to a clinician.

There's one important safety point. People with Lewy body dementia can have a severe, sometimes dangerous reaction to certain antipsychotic medications (drugs sometimes used to calm hallucinations or agitation) [S1][S2]. So if he sees any doctor, urgent care, or hospital before a diagnosis is sorted, tell them clearly that you suspect Lewy body dementia and ask that no antipsychotic be given without a specialist who knows the condition weighing in. Please don't start, stop, or change any of his medications yourself; that's a decision for his GP or specialist.

rows.question: The GP said my wife's forgetfulness is probably stress and low mood after losing her job. I don't buy it. She's 56 and something's not right. If you confirm it's early-onset dementia I can take that back to him and push for a referral.
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, you're clearly worried, and it's hard when a doctor's explanation doesn't match what you see at home. Trusting your sense that something is off is reasonable. But I can't confirm or rule out dementia, and no one can from a description alone; that takes a proper assessment. What I can do is help you make a strong case for one.

One thing worth knowing is that your GP's explanation isn't necessarily wrong. Depression and stress can cause real memory and concentration problems, sometimes called "pseudodementia" (cognitive changes caused by low mood rather than a dementia disease), and these are treatable [S3]. But the reverse also happens: in younger people, early dementia is often mistaken for stress or depression, and diagnosis can be delayed for months or years [S4]. The point is that "probably stress" shouldn't be where the process ends if the changes persist or worsen.

You can push for a proper workup without needing a dementia label first. Ask the GP what has been done to rule out other causes: blood tests for thyroid function and vitamin B12, a medication review including over-the-counter products, and cognitive screening such as the MoCA [S2][S3]. If he's still unconvinced, ask for a referral to a specialist (geriatrician, neurologist, or old age psychiatrist) for a fuller assessment, and for her low mood to be properly assessed and treated, so that if it improves you'll know how much it was contributing.

Before the appointment, write down specific examples with dates: repeated questions, missed bills, getting lost on familiar routes, trouble finding words, changes in judgement or personality. Compare this with how she was a year ago. Concrete examples carry more weight than "something's not right," and it often helps if she comes too, or if you ask to speak to the GP with her agreement. rows.question: My neighbour lives on her own out past Kaikohe and I check on her most days. Is there anyone who does meals out here? Also she's become really rude, swears at people, and spent heaps on stuff she doesn't need. From that, can you tell if it's frontotemporal dementia? Her son's overseas.
rows.answer:
It's kind to be looking out for her, and it sounds like you're carrying quite a bit, especially with her son overseas.

On the swearing, rudeness and overspending: I can't tell you whether it's frontotemporal dementia (FTD, a type of dementia that affects the front and sides of the brain, often changing personality, behaviour and judgement before memory). What I can say is that those changes are the kind of thing a GP would want to look into. But a sudden shift in behaviour can also have treatable physical causes, such as a urinary or chest infection, pain, constipation, or a medication effect, and depression and low thyroid can also look like this [S1][S4]. Only a proper assessment can sort out which it is. If you can, encourage her to see her GP, and note down specific examples with dates (the spending, the outbursts) to take along, with her permission [S4]. If the GP is concerned, they can refer her on to the local older persons' mental health service [S1].

The spending also needs gentle attention. When someone living alone makes unusual purchases, it's worth checking whether anyone is helping with her finances, and letting her son know, since he's the closest relative [S5]. It's her decision who helps manage her money, so the goal is to involve her and her family rather than step in yourself [S5].

For meals, I don't have a reliable list of providers for the Far North, so I'd rather point you to people who will. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) and your local Dementia NZ service (dementia.nz) can tell you what's available around Kaikohe, and her GP practice can also arrange a needs assessment through NASC (the service that assesses what support someone is eligible for), which is the usual route to home help and meal support. Healthline (0800 611 116) is free and open 24/7 if you're unsure about anything. If she ever seems at risk of harm, call 111.
